question: A tank endorsement is required for a Class A or B CDL if a driver wants to haul a liquid or liquid gas in a tank with what minimum capacity thresholds?
choice_a: Individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more
choice_b: Any tank used to carry liquid, regardless of size
choice_c: Individual rated capacity of more than 50 gallons regardless of aggregate
choice_d: Aggregate rated capacity of 500 gallons or more only
explanation: A tank endorsement is required if the vehicle needs a Class A or B CDL and hauls liquid or liquid gas in a tank or tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Introduction

question: On all tank vehicles, what is the most important item to check for during inspection?
explanation: On all tank vehicles, the most important item to check for is leaks; check under and around the vehicle for signs of leaking.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.1.1, Leaks

question: What does the manual say about carrying liquids or gases in a leaking tank?
choice_a: Doing so is a crime; the driver will be cited and prevented from driving further, and may be liable for spill clean-up
choice_b: It is acceptable for short trips of under 50 miles
choice_c: It is only prohibited for hazardous materials
choice_d: It is permitted if the driver notifies dispatch first
explanation: Don't carry liquids or gases in a leaking tank -- to do so is a crime; the driver will be cited and prevented from driving further, and may also be liable for the clean-up of any spill.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.1.1, Leaks

question: What must a driver never do regarding valves and manhole covers on a tank vehicle?
choice_a: There is no specific rule about valves or manhole covers while driving
choice_b: Never close manhole covers before driving
choice_c: Always leave the manhole cover slightly open for ventilation
choice_d: Never drive with open valves or manhole covers
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers, and to check that manhole covers have gaskets and close correctly and that vents are clear.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.1.1, Leaks

question: Which of the following is listed as special purpose equipment a driver should check if the vehicle has it?
choice_b: Vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher
explanation: If the vehicle has vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, or a built-in fire extinguisher, the driver must make sure they work.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.1.2, Check Special Purpose Equipment

question: Why are liquid tankers especially easy to roll over?
choice_a: Because much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, making the vehicle top-heavy
choice_b: Because tank vehicles are lighter than dry van trailers
choice_c: Because tank vehicles have fewer axles than other combination vehicles
explanation: A high center of gravity means much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, making the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over; tests have shown tankers can turn over at speed limits posted for curves.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.2.1, High Center of Gravity

question: What is "liquid surge" and why is it dangerous?
choice_a: A sudden increase in engine RPM caused by tank pressure
choice_b: The pressure buildup inside a fully sealed, completely full tank
choice_c: A type of electrical surge in the ABS system
choice_d: Movement of liquid in partially filled tanks that can push the truck in the direction the wave is moving, even shoving a stopped truck into an intersection on ice
explanation: Liquid surge results from movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks; when a wave hits the end of the tank, it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving, and on a slippery surface like ice, it can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.2.2, Danger of Surge

question: When loading and unloading a liquid tank divided into smaller tanks by bulkheads, what must the driver pay attention to?
choice_a: Weight distribution, so as not to put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle
choice_c: The type of fifth wheel installed
explanation: Some liquid tanks are divided into several smaller tanks by bulkheads; when loading and unloading the smaller tanks, the driver must pay attention to weight distribution and avoid putting too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.2.3, Bulkheads

question: What do baffled liquid tanks do, and what surge risk remains even with baffles?
choice_a: Baffles eliminate all liquid surge in every direction
choice_b: Baffles have holes that help control forward and backward surge, but side-to-side surge can still occur and can cause a rollover
choice_c: Baffles are only used in un-baffled smooth bore tanks
explanation: Baffled liquid tanks have bulkheads in them with holes that let liquid flow through, helping control forward and backward surge; side-to-side surge can still occur, which can cause a rollover.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.2.4, Baffled Tanks

question: What are un-baffled liquid tankers ("smooth bore" tanks) commonly used to transport, and why do they lack baffles?
choice_a: Fuel oil, since baffles increase fire risk
choice_b: Dry bulk goods, since baffles are unnecessary for solids
choice_c: Food products like milk, since sanitation regulations forbid baffles because of the difficulty in cleaning the inside of the tank
choice_d: Hazardous chemicals, since baffles would react with them
explanation: Un-baffled tanks are usually those that transport food products such as milk, since sanitation regulations forbid the use of baffles due to the difficulty of cleaning the inside of the tank; forward-and-back surge in these tanks is very strong.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.2.5, Un-baffled Tanks

question: What is "outage" in the context of loading a cargo tank?
choice_a: The room that must be left for liquid to expand as it warms, since a cargo tank should never be loaded totally full
choice_b: The amount of fuel used during a delivery route
choice_c: A term for a leak that has already occurred
choice_d: The distance a tank vehicle travels between fill-ups
explanation: Never load a cargo tank totally full; liquids expand as they warm and room must be left for the expanding liquid, called "outage." Different liquids expand by different amounts, requiring different outage.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.2.6, Outage

question: What three factors determine how much of a dense liquid, such as some acids, can legally be loaded into a tank?
choice_a: The amount the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits
choice_b: The color of the placard and the shipper's paperwork only
choice_c: Only the driver's personal preference and the tank's total volume
choice_d: Only the distance to be traveled
explanation: A full tank of dense liquid may exceed legal weight limits; the amount of liquid to load depends on the amount the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.2.7, How Much to Load

question: What braking practice helps control surge when driving a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Keep steady pressure on the brakes and do not release too soon when coming to a stop, braking far in advance and increasing following distance
choice_b: Release the brakes completely the instant the vehicle begins to slow
choice_c: Use only the parking brake for all stops
choice_d: Pump the brakes rapidly and repeatedly when approaching a stop
explanation: To control surge, keep a steady pressure on the brakes, do not release too soon when coming to a stop, brake far in advance of a stop, and increase following distance.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.3.2, Controlling Surge

question: How should a driver approach curves in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Maintain a constant speed matching the posted limit throughout
choice_b: Curves should always be taken at highway speed if the tank is baffled
choice_c: Slow down before the curve, then accelerate slightly through the curve, since the posted speed may be too fast for a tank vehicle
choice_d: Accelerate before the curve and brake through it
explanation: Slow down before curves, then accelerate slightly through the curve; the posted speed for a curve may be too fast for a tank vehicle.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.3.3, Curves

question: According to the manual, which tank vehicles may take longer to stop -- empty or full?
choice_a: Empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones
choice_b: Full tank vehicles always take longer to stop than empty ones
choice_c: Load level has no effect on tank vehicle stopping distance
choice_d: Only baffled tanks have this issue
explanation: The manual notes that wet roads double the normal stopping distance, and empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.3.4, Stopping Distance

question: What driving behaviors does the manual warn against to avoid skids in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Using the emergency line shut-off valve
choice_b: Checking the manhole covers before driving
choice_d: Over steering, over accelerating, or over braking
explanation: Don't over steer, over accelerate, or over brake -- doing so may cause the vehicle to skid; on tank trailers, if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid, the vehicle may jackknife.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.3.5, Skids

question: According to the Kentucky manual, how many questions are on the Tankers endorsement knowledge test?
explanation: The Kentucky manual states the Tankers endorsement knowledge test consists of 20 questions, with 80 percent correct required to pass, per 49 CFR 383.135(a).
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Testing Requirements

question: Why must a driver start, slow down, and stop very smoothly in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Because tank vehicles are exempt from normal speed limits
choice_b: Because of the high center of gravity and the surge of the liquid
choice_c: Because tank vehicles have weaker brakes than dry vans
choice_d: Smooth driving is only a fuel-economy recommendation for tankers
explanation: Because of the high center of gravity and the surge of the liquid, a driver must start, slow down, and stop very smoothly, and also make smooth turns and lane changes.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 8, Tank Vehicles, Subsection 8.3.1, Drive Smoothly
